opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a good question, and I'm not sure I'd frame it as a trade-off so much as two things that are pretty deeply intertwined. In some sense, almost everything we do on the measurement side is in service of forecasting. Nobody really cares that much about whether a model can complete some particular software task today for its own sake. What we care about is: what does this tell us about where things are going, and how much time do we have before models can do things that would really matter, like substantially automating AI research or doing things that are dangerous?

That said, there's a real tension in how you design the work. If you're focused purely on measuring current capabilities, you want tasks that are really well-calibrated to where models are right now, so you get a lot of signal and can distinguish between, say, two frontier models. But if you're trying to forecast, you need measurements that stay meaningful over time. You need some kind of consistent scale that you can track across many generations of models, because the trend is the thing you're extrapolating. That pushes you toward building a range of tasks, from very easy to really hard, and toward metrics that have some intuitive interpretation, like the length of task, measured in how long it takes a skilled human, that a model can complete with some reliability. That metric is useful precisely because you can plot it over several years and ask what the trend looks like.

The flip side is that the more you lean into forecasting, the more you're making assumptions that are hard to validate. Does performance on our task suite actually transfer to messy real-world work? Is the trend going to continue, speed up, or hit some wall? So I think a lot of our work is in going back and forth: making careful measurements now, then checking whether those measurements actually correspond to things we care about in the real world, for example by comparing benchmark-style tasks with more realistic settings, and being pretty honest about the gaps.

So I'd say measurement is the foundation, and forecasting is the main reason we do it. The trade-off mostly shows up in resource allocation and in how much uncertainty we're willing to put on the claims we make about the future.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that we don't really see those as being in tension most of the time, because the way we try to forecast is by measuring. Like, the time horizon work is a good example. The headline result is this doubling time, which is a forecasting claim about where things are going, but you can't get that without first doing a lot of pretty unglamorous measurement of what models can actually do right now on tasks of various lengths. So the measurement is the thing that makes the forecasting possible at all.

Where I think there is a real trade-off is in what you choose to measure. If all you care about is "what can the current model do," you'd build evals that are very targeted at the frontier, really hard tasks, lots of resolution right where models are struggling today. But if you want a trend line that extends backwards and forwards, you need tasks that span a huge range of difficulty, including stuff that's trivially easy for current models and stuff that's way out of reach. And that's kind of annoying, because a lot of that effort goes into tasks that aren't going to tell you anything interesting about this particular model. It only pays off because it lets you fit a curve.

The other thing I'd say is that there's a kind of epistemic trade-off. When we just report "here's what we observed when we ran the model on these tasks," that's pretty defensible, we can show our work. The moment you say "and therefore in two years we expect X," you're bringing in a lot of assumptions, like that the trend continues, that the tasks we picked are representative of the thing people actually care about, that there's no weird discontinuity. I'm personally more comfortable on the measurement side, and I think a lot of us at METR are. But I also think that if we only did measurement and refused to extrapolate, we'd be leaving the forecasting to people who are doing it with less data than we have, which seems worse. So we try to be really explicit about the uncertainty when we do extrapolate, and keep the raw measurements front and center so people can disagree with our forecast without having to disagree with our data.

astra-6.text:
I think those are pretty closely connected. Ultimately, a lot of what we care about is forward-looking: when might AI systems be able to do things that have substantial consequences, and how much time do we have to prepare? But to make useful forecasts, you need a good understanding of what systems can do today, and how that’s changed over time.

So I wouldn’t frame it as choosing between measuring capabilities and forecasting progress. Measurement gives you a basis for forecasting, and the forecasting questions help you decide what’s worth measuring. If you care about systems being able to carry out long, complicated tasks, you want evaluations that tell you something about that, rather than just whether they can answer a particular set of questions.

There is still a resource trade-off. You can spend more time understanding the limitations of a current system, or more time thinking about how to extrapolate. And a good measurement doesn’t automatically give you a good forecast. You still have to ask whether the trend will continue, whether your tasks are representative, and whether something important is missing from the evaluation. I think the useful thing is to make those assumptions explicit, rather than treating an evaluation score as a prediction by itself.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of those as pretty closely connected. If you want to forecast AI progress, you need a good understanding of what systems can do today and how that’s changed over time. And if you want to measure current capabilities, you need some view about which capabilities are going to matter as systems get more powerful.

There is still a trade-off in where you spend your effort. You could spend more time making a measurement of today’s systems really robust, or you could spend that time exploring tasks that current systems mostly fail at but that might become informative later. I think you want some of both.

The thing I’d be cautious about is treating a current capability measurement as though it directly gives you a forecast. There are additional assumptions involved—about whether the trend continues, whether your tasks remain representative, and what changes in how people build and use these systems. So measurements can provide an empirical foundation for forecasting, but they don’t eliminate the uncertainty.
